title: Every Risk Has an Owner, and the Contract Decides Who
summary: A construction contract is mostly a machine for deciding who pays when something goes wrong. The sound principle is to give each risk to the party best able to control it, price it and carry it. This lesson sets out that principle and the six tools the week will study.
body:
A construction contract is mostly a machine for deciding who pays when something goes wrong. Give each risk to the party who can best control it, price it and carry it, and pay openly for every risk you move.

Recall

Q. What is a time bar in a construction contract?

A. A clause that cuts off a claim if notice is not given within a stated period. Under some contracts and in some courts it is enforced strictly, so a late notice can lose a good claim outright.

Q. What is a handshake deal, and why did Week 75 treat it as a failure pattern?

A. An agreement between partners that was never written down. It works while everyone agrees and fails when value rises, because each side then remembers the terms in its own favour.

Q. In Week 70, what made a share of a deal a security?

A. In substance, money invested in a common enterprise with an expectation of profit from the efforts of others. The label on the document did not decide it; the economic reality did.

Why this matters

Mr Shabazz, most of the money lost on construction projects is not lost because something went wrong. Things always go wrong. It is lost because nobody had agreed in advance who would pay when they did. Rock under the footings, a supplier that fails, a storm in the month you pour the roof slab, a consultant's drawing error: each of these has a cost, and the contract either names the party who carries it or leaves the question to a dispute. A dispute is the most expensive way ever invented to allocate a risk.

As the owner, you write the first draft of that allocation. Whatever you put in the tender documents, every bidder prices. Push a risk onto a party who cannot manage it and you do not get rid of it. You buy it back, at a markup, in the bid price, and then you pay for it again when the party you pushed it onto fails.

The allocation principle

In plain English: give the risk to whoever can do the most about it.

The professional framing is the allocation test, which has three questions. Who can control the risk, meaning reduce its likelihood or its size? Who can price it, meaning estimate it well enough to put a sensible number in a bid? Who can carry it, meaning survive the loss if it happens without collapsing? The best owner of a risk passes all three. Where no party passes all three, the answer is usually to share it, or to buy insurance, which is a market that exists to carry risks nobody on the project should carry alone.

Apply it. The contractor controls workmanship, the sequence of work and the safety of the site, and can price them from experience, so those risks sit with the contractor. The owner controls the brief, the design team it hires and the timing of its own decisions, so design changes and late owner instructions sit with the owner. Ground conditions are the classic hard case. Nobody controls the ground. The owner knows more about it, because it commissioned the site investigation and has owned the land for months. The contractor has only a few weeks of tender time to read the report. That is why many standard forms leave unforeseen ground with the owner, and why owners who strip that protection out pay for it.

A worked example, with hypothetical round numbers. A 10,000,000 dollar lump-sum contract for a mid-rise building. Under the first version of the contract, unforeseen ground is the owner's risk: if the contractor meets conditions materially different from the site report, it is paid the extra cost. Under the second version, the contractor accepts all ground risk. A careful bidder looking at the second version adds a premium for the risk it cannot see, say 400,000 dollars. Now suppose the ground is fine. Under version one the owner pays 10,000,000 dollars. Under version two it pays 10,400,000 dollars for nothing. Suppose instead the ground holds rock that costs 600,000 dollars to remove. Under version one the owner pays 10,600,000 dollars. Under version two, a bidder who priced nothing because it wanted the job is now 600,000 dollars down on a contract with a thin margin, and starts looking for any argument to recover it. The cheap transfer was not cheap.

Say that out loud now.

A risk you push onto someone who cannot carry it comes back to you, with interest.

The six tools of the week

Contracts move risk with a small set of tools, and this week takes each in turn.

  • An indemnity: a promise by one party to make good another's loss from a defined cause, often including claims by third parties.
  • A limitation of liability: a cap on how much one party can be made to pay in total, or for a type of loss.
  • A consequential loss exclusion: a clause removing liability for indirect losses, such as lost profit or lost rent, which are often far larger than the direct cost of a defect.
  • An unforeseen ground clause, often called a differing site conditions clause: it decides who pays when the ground is not what the investigation showed.
  • Force majeure: relief from the consequences of extraordinary events neither party controls, usually time and sometimes money.
  • Liquidated damages: a fixed sum per day or week that the contractor pays the owner for late completion, agreed in advance in place of proving the actual loss.

Notice that every tool works on two axes: what is covered, and how much. A wide indemnity with a low cap can be worth less than a narrow one with no cap. Read every risk clause for both.

A second worked example, hypothetical. A design consultant's error causes a 2,000,000 dollar loss. The consultant's appointment caps liability at its fee of 300,000 dollars and excludes consequential loss. Of the 2,000,000 dollars, 1,200,000 dollars is direct rework and 800,000 dollars is lost rent from a late opening. The exclusion removes the 800,000 dollars. The cap then limits recovery on the 1,200,000 dollars to 300,000 dollars. The owner carries 1,700,000 dollars of a loss caused entirely by someone else. Nothing in that outcome is unusual; it is what the clauses said. The time to change it was at appointment, not after the error.

How the best do it

Sophisticated owners decide the allocation before anyone drafts a clause. They build a risk allocation matrix: one row per significant risk, one column per party, and a note for each on control, pricing and capacity to carry. The lawyers then draft to the matrix, and the tender documents explain it so every bidder prices the same risks. A small developer can copy this with one page and twenty rows. The point is not the format. It is that allocation becomes a decision you made, rather than a surprise you inherited from a form.

Six-Lens Check

Tax: whether a payment under an indemnity or liquidated damages is income, a reduction of cost or something else depends on local rules; verify that against the primary source before you rely on it. Liability: the allocation decides which entity ends up with a loss, so keep risk inside the project vehicle, not above it. Banking: lenders read the risk clauses and size contingency against what the owner retained. Governance: record who approved each departure from the standard form, and why. Estate: a personal indemnity can outlive the project and bind your estate. Exit: a buyer or refinancing lender will ask what claims and indemnities survive completion.

Professional sign-off required: lawyer, as construction counsel; insurance broker, on which risks can be insured instead of transferred.

The biggest risk

The biggest risk is the illusion of transfer: believing that because a clause moves a risk onto the contractor, it has left your project. If the contractor cannot carry it, it returns as a claim, a dispute or an insolvency. The control is the three-question test, applied in writing, before the tender goes out.

The beginner's mistake

The beginner takes a standard form and adds owner-friendly amendments everywhere, assuming each one saves money. Bidders read those amendments and price them. Ask of every amendment: what will this add to the bid, and what will it cost me if the contractor cannot honour it?

Callback

In Week 52, Marco taught that the delivery method you choose, design-bid-build, design-build or construction management, already decides much of the risk allocation before a single clause is written. This week drills into the clauses. The two must agree: a design-build contract that leaves design risk with the owner, or a design-bid-build contract that pushes design risk onto a contractor who did not design, is a contract at war with itself.

Recap

Every risk on a project has an owner, and the contract names it. The sound owner can control, price and carry the risk. Six tools move risk: indemnities, limitations of liability, consequential loss exclusions, unforeseen ground clauses, force majeure and liquidated damages. Read each for what it covers and for how much.

Next: Ford, with Cole, on Failure Forensics: a composite case of the ground clause that transferred everything.
checklist: I have a one-page risk allocation matrix before the tender documents go out.
For each major risk I can say who controls it, who can price it and who can carry it.
I know which risks the standard form leaves with me and why.
I have asked what each owner-friendly amendment will add to the bid price.
I read every risk clause for what it covers and for how much.
I know the cap and the consequential loss position in every consultant appointment.
I have asked my broker which risks can be insured rather than transferred.

terms: Risk allocation — the contract's decision about which party bears the cost and time consequences of each identified risk.
Indemnity — a promise by one party to make good another's loss from a defined cause, often including third-party claims.
Limitation of liability — a clause capping the total amount, or the amount for a type of loss, that a party can be made to pay.

hostile.q: Your draft contract has no differing site conditions clause. Why should I not add a ground-risk premium to my bid?
hostile.a: You are right to ask, and we have reversed that draft position. You will get the full geotechnical report, the extra boreholes we commissioned and a defined baseline. If the ground differs materially from that baseline, the cost is ours. We are keeping the risk because we know more about the ground than you can in a tender period, and we do not want to pay a premium for a risk you cannot see.

title: The Ground Clause That Transferred Everything
summary: A composite case: an owner struck the unforeseen ground clause from a lump-sum contract and took the lowest bid, from a contractor that had priced no ground risk at all. When the ground turned out bad, the risk came back as claims, delay, insolvency and a second contractor's price. Seven forensic steps show where it could have been stopped.
body:
This is a composite example. An owner pushed all ground risk onto the lowest bidder, the ground was bad, and the risk the owner thought it had transferred came back larger than it would ever have been if the owner had kept it.

Recall

Q. What are the three questions of the allocation test?

A. Who can control the risk, who can price it and who can carry it. The best owner of a risk passes all three; where nobody does, share it or insure it.

Q. In Week 77, what does an order of precedence clause do?

A. It ranks the contract documents, such as the agreement, the conditions, the specifications and the drawings, so that when two of them conflict, the higher-ranked one governs.

Q. In Week 70, what is a resale restriction on a security?

A. A limit on when and how an investor who bought under an exemption may sell the security on, so that an exempt sale does not become a back door to the public market.

Why this matters

Mr Shabazz, Cole joins me today because this failure is a legal one dressed as an engineering one. The ground did nothing unusual; ground never does. What failed was a contract that pretended the owner could get rid of a risk by deleting a clause. The numbers are hypothetical round figures, and the story is assembled from patterns that recur on real projects.

1. Timeline

An owner tenders a 20,000,000 dollar lump-sum contract for a building on a former industrial site. The owner's lawyer deletes the standard differing site conditions clause and adds a clause stating that the contractor has satisfied itself as to all ground conditions and accepts all risk. Five bids arrive. Four include ground contingencies of between 800,000 and 1,200,000 dollars. The fifth is 900,000 dollars below the next lowest and includes none. The owner awards to the fifth. In month 3, excavation finds buried foundations from an old structure and soft clay below the depth the site investigation reached. Piles must be added. The contractor submits a claim for 2,500,000 dollars and four months of extra time. The owner rejects it under the risk clause. The contractor slows the work. By month 9 it is in dispute, short of cash and behind on subcontractor payments. In month 11 it fails. A replacement contractor prices the remaining work, including the piles, at a figure far above the original contract balance.

2. Key decisions

Three decisions mattered. Deleting the ground clause and replacing it with a blanket acceptance of risk. Awarding to a bid that was an outlier by almost a million dollars without asking why. And meeting the first ground claim with a flat refusal under the clause, rather than with an engineering review of what had actually been found.

3. Assumptions

The owner assumed that a clause transferring risk would be enforced exactly as written. Cole's point is that this is not guaranteed. Courts in some places read a blanket risk clause against the party that relied on it, especially where the owner held information it did not disclose, or where the site report was misleading; verify that against the primary source before you rely on it. The owner also assumed the contractor would absorb the loss quietly. A contractor 2,500,000 dollars down on a 20,000,000 dollar job does not absorb anything. It looks for a way out.

4. Incentives

The owner's lawyer was rewarded for drafting the most owner-protective document possible, not for the price that document produced or the dispute it invited. The winning contractor wanted the work badly enough to bid without contingency and hope. The owner's project team wanted the lowest number to show the investment committee. Every party was rational. Nobody was paid to ask whether the risk had gone anywhere real.

Say that out loud now.

A deleted clause does not delete the ground.

5. Warning signs ignored

The site investigation stopped at a shallow depth on a site with a known industrial history. The bid spread showed four contractors pricing ground risk and one not. The low bidder's tender qualifications were silent on ground, which on a site like this is itself a statement. In month 3 the first claim came with photographs and borehole logs, not opinion. In month 6 subcontractors started complaining of slow payment, the classic sign of a contractor running short of cash.

6. Point of no return

The point of no return was month 6. Up to then, the owner could have negotiated: commissioned an independent geotechnical review, agreed a measured payment for the piles under a change, and kept a solvent contractor on site. That would have cost something near the 1,000,000 dollars the other bidders had priced. After month 6, the contractor's cash position had gone, and every option left involved a second contractor, a remobilisation and a dispute running in parallel.

7. Root cause

The root cause was not the clay or the buried foundations. It was a contract that moved a risk onto a party that could not control it, could not price it in the time allowed and could not carry it if it happened. The allocation failed all three questions of the test. The money saved at award was never real. It was a loan from the future, taken at a punishing rate.

Cole's view: why the clause did not protect the owner

Cole reads the file as an auditor would. First, the clause was only as strong as the owner's disclosure. If the owner held earlier reports of buried structures and did not provide them, a claim of misrepresentation or non-disclosure could sit outside the risk clause altogether. Second, even a clause that is perfectly enforceable is worth only what the contractor can pay. A judgment against an insolvent company is a piece of paper. Third, the owner's own records were thin: no log of what information was given to bidders and when, and no record of why the outlier bid was accepted. In the dispute that followed, the owner could not prove what it had disclosed.

A second worked example, hypothetical, on what the owner actually paid. Original contract 20,000,000 dollars. Paid to the failed contractor before insolvency: 9,000,000 dollars. Replacement contractor's price to finish, including piles and remobilisation: 14,500,000 dollars. Owner's own extra costs for delay, interest and fees: 1,500,000 dollars. Total outturn: 25,000,000 dollars, against 21,000,000 dollars if it had awarded to the next lowest bid with ground contingency included. The deleted clause cost the owner about 4,000,000 dollars.

The prevention rule

Rule 78: Never transfer a risk to a party that cannot control it, price it or carry it; keep risks you understand better than the bidder, disclose everything you hold, and pay for every risk you move.

Professional sign-off required: geotechnical engineer, on the scope of site investigation before tender; lawyer, on the ground risk clause and the disclosure record.

The biggest risk

The biggest risk is mistaking a drafting victory for a risk reduction. The control is to ask, before any risk clause goes into a tender, whether the receiving party can do anything about the risk, and what happens to you if it cannot pay.

The beginner's mistake

The beginner celebrates the lowest bid. An outlier bid is a question, not a prize. Ask the bidder, in writing, what it has assumed about the risks the others priced, and record the answer.

Callback

In Week 31, Pax and Cole taught geotechnical desk diligence as part of site due diligence. This case shows what that diligence is for. The investigation you commission before you buy the land is the same document you hand to bidders, and its depth sets the boundary between the risk you can define and the risk nobody can price.

Recap

An owner deleted the ground clause, took an outlier bid with no ground contingency and refused the first claim. The contractor failed, and the outturn exceeded the next lowest bid by about 4,000,000 dollars. The root cause was a transfer that failed every question of the allocation test. Rule 78 keeps risks with the party that can manage them.

Next: Roman on The Money: how risk allocation shows up in the bid price, the contingency and the lender's view.
checklist: I scope the site investigation to the depth and history of the site before tender.
I give every bidder everything I hold on the ground, and I keep a dated record of what I gave.
I compare ground contingencies across bids and treat an outlier as a question.
I ask any outlier bidder in writing what it assumed about risks the others priced.
I meet a first claim with an engineering review, not a flat refusal.
I watch subcontractor payment complaints as an early sign of contractor cash stress.
I compare the saving from a risk transfer with the cost of the transferee failing.

The contractor claimed, the owner refused under the clause, the contractor slowed, ran short of cash and failed in month 11. With a replacement contractor, delay and fees, the outturn reached about 25,000,000 dollars, against 21,000,000 if the owner had taken the next bid. terms: Differing site conditions clause — a clause that pays the contractor when the ground or existing conditions differ materially from what the contract documents showed.
Outlier bid — a bid far from the others, which usually means the bidder has priced a different scope or a different risk.
Non-disclosure — failing to give the other party information you hold that bears on the risk it is being asked to carry.

hostile.q: Your contract says the contractor accepted all ground risk. Why are you negotiating my claim at all?
hostile.a: Because a clause is only worth what the other side can pay, and because I want my building finished, not a judgment against an insolvent company. I will commission an independent geotechnical review of what was found against what our report showed. Where the conditions are within what a competent bidder should have expected, the cost stays with you. Where they are materially outside it, I would rather agree a measured price now than fund a dispute and a second contractor later.

rule: Rule 78: Never transfer a risk to a party that cannot control it, price it or carry it; keep risks you understand better than the bidder, disclose everything you hold, and pay for every risk you move.

title: Every Transferred Risk Has a Price Tag
summary: A risk moved onto a contractor or consultant is never free: it comes back as a premium in the price. Comparing that premium with the expected cost of keeping the risk tells you whether the transfer is worth buying. The lender then sizes contingency against what you kept.
body:
Every risk you move onto someone else comes back to you as a premium in their price. The money question is simple: is the premium smaller than the expected cost of keeping the risk, plus the cost of the other party failing to pay?

Recall

Q. What was Rule 78?

A. Never transfer a risk to a party that cannot control it, price it or carry it; keep risks you understand better than the bidder, disclose everything you hold, and pay for every risk you move.

Q. In Week 77, what is a condition precedent to a claim?

A. A requirement, usually notice within a time limit and in a stated form, that must be met before a party is entitled to extra time or money. Miss it and the entitlement may be lost.

Q. In Week 70, why does selling to the wrong investor matter even if the project succeeds?

A. Because a sale outside an exemption can give investors a right to unwind their purchase or claim damages, and can expose the issuer to regulatory sanctions, whatever the outcome of the project.

Why this matters

Mr Shabazz, a contract negotiation looks like an argument about words. It is really an argument about money, settled in advance. Every clause that moves a risk changes the price you pay today, the contingency you must carry, and the size of the loan a lender will offer. If you cannot put a number on a clause, you cannot decide whether to fight for it.

Expected cost: the number behind a risk

In plain English: a risk is worth roughly how likely it is times how much it would cost.

The professional framing is expected value: probability multiplied by impact, summed across the ways a risk can play out. It is a long-run average, not a forecast of what will happen on your project. On any single job the risk either happens or it does not. But expected value is the right yardstick for comparing the price of transferring a risk with the cost of keeping it.

A worked example, with hypothetical round numbers. On a 15,000,000 dollar project, your geotechnical engineer judges a 20 percent chance that ground conditions will need extra foundation work costing 1,000,000 dollars, and a 5 percent chance of a worse case costing 3,000,000 dollars. Expected cost of keeping the risk: 0.20 times 1,000,000 plus 0.05 times 3,000,000, which is 200,000 plus 150,000, or 350,000 dollars. Now the bids. If you transfer ground risk, the competent bidders add between 600,000 and 900,000 dollars. They add more than the expected cost, and they are right to: they cannot diversify the risk across many sites the way a large insurer can, they have less information than you, and they need a margin for carrying it. Paying 750,000 dollars to avoid an expected 350,000 dollar cost is a poor trade unless you cannot survive the 3,000,000 dollar case.

That last condition is the whole point. Expected value tells you the average. Your balance sheet tells you whether you can live through the bad tail. Transfer a risk when the tail would break you. Keep it when you can carry the tail and the premium is rich.

Say that out loud now.

Keep the risk when I can carry the bad case. Pay to move it when I cannot.

The credit discount on a transfer

A transfer is only worth what the other party can pay. That turns every risk clause into a credit question.

A second worked example, hypothetical. You negotiate an indemnity from a subcontractor for a 2,000,000 dollar exposure. The subcontractor has net assets of 400,000 dollars and liability insurance of 1,000,000 dollars that may or may not respond to that loss. The realistic value of the indemnity is the insurance that actually responds plus what you could collect from the company, perhaps 1,000,000 to 1,400,000 dollars on a good day, and less after legal costs. If you were paying a 150,000 dollar premium in the price for the full 2,000,000 dollar transfer, you were overpaying for protection that was never fully there. The fix is to price the indemnity against the counterparty's real capacity: require insurance with limits that match the exposure, check the policy actually covers the risk, and ask for a bond or parent guarantee where the company is thin.

The middle path: share the risk in bands

Transfer and retention are not the only choices. Many risks are better shared in bands. A common commercial structure for ground risk is a baseline: the contractor carries the cost of conditions up to a defined level, written into the contract from the site investigation, and the owner pays for anything materially worse. Another is a shared overrun band, where the owner and contractor split cost above a target in agreed proportions up to a ceiling.

Run the hypothetical numbers again. If the contractor carries the first 300,000 dollars of ground cost and the owner carries the rest, the contractor's premium falls, because its tail is now capped and it can price a bounded number. The owner's retained exposure is the severe case less 300,000 dollars, which its contingency and equity can be sized against. Each party carries the slice it can manage. These structures are commercial practice, not standards, and each needs careful drafting of the baseline.

How the lender reads your allocation

The lender sees the same contract and asks one question: what did the owner keep? Every risk you retained must be covered by contingency, by equity or by a guarantee. A lender's monitor will read the risk clauses and recommend a contingency that reflects them. Keep ground risk and the monitor will look for a ground allowance. Accept liquidated damages capped at a low figure and the lender will model your interest carry for the delay beyond the cap, because that is now yours.

Take that last point to numbers, hypothetically. Liquidated damages are 5,000 dollars a day, capped at 10 percent of a 15,000,000 dollar contract, so 1,500,000 dollars, which covers 300 days. If the owner's true daily cost of delay, in interest, fees and lost rent, is 8,000 dollars, then each day of contractor delay leaves 3,000 dollars with the owner even before the cap is reached. The lender notices that gap. So should you. These caps, rates and percentages are commercial practice negotiated deal by deal, not standards.

The Wealth Ledger

Warrick's note for your personal balance sheet. Risk allocation is where a project problem either stays inside the project company or climbs up to you. A risk the project retained is covered by project contingency and project equity. A risk that the project cannot cover, and that sits behind a personal guarantee or a personal indemnity you signed, is a liability on your own balance sheet, contingent until the day it is called. Keep a list of every personal promise that stands behind a project risk, with its cap and its end date, and review it every quarter. Your liquidity floor from Week 7 should be sized with that list in mind. A licensed adviser is required before you act on any personal financial decision.

The biggest risk

The biggest risk is paying for protection that is not there: a premium in the price for a transfer to a party with no capacity to honour it. The control is to price every transfer against the receiving party's insurance, assets and security, and to verify the insurance responds to that specific loss.

The beginner's mistake

The beginner compares the premium with the worst case and concludes the transfer is cheap. Compare the premium with the expected cost, then ask separately whether you could survive the worst case. Those are two different questions, and both need an answer.

Callback

In Week 44, I taught stress tests: base, downside and severe cases, and the break-evens behind them. This lesson applies the same discipline to a single clause. Run the expected cost for the base view, the severe case for survival, and decide the allocation by asking which case would break the project.

Recap

A transferred risk comes back as a premium. Compare it with the expected cost of keeping the risk, then ask whether you could carry the bad case. Discount any transfer by the receiving party's capacity to pay. The lender sizes contingency to what you kept, so your allocation sets your budget.

Next: LEX on The Rules: how courts read indemnities, caps, consequential loss and liquidated damages.
checklist: I estimate the expected cost of each major risk with my engineer before tender.
I compare each risk premium in the bids with that expected cost.
I ask separately whether the project could survive the worst case of each risk.
I check the receiving party's insurance, assets and security before valuing any transfer.
I confirm the insurance would actually respond to the risk being transferred.
I compare the liquidated damages rate with my true daily cost of delay.
I keep a list of every personal promise that stands behind a project risk.

speak: Every risk I move onto someone else comes back as a premium in their price. So I put a number on it. Expected cost is probability times impact: a 20 percent chance of 1,000,000 dollars and a 5 percent chance of 3,000,000 dollars is an expected 350,000. If bidders want 750,000 to take that risk, I keep it, unless the 3,000,000 dollar case would break the project. Expected value tells me the average; my balance sheet tells me whether I survive the tail. Then the credit question: a transfer is worth only what the other side can pay, so I value it against their insurance and assets. And the lender sizes contingency to what I kept. If liquidated damages are 5,000 dollars a day and my true delay cost is 8,000, the 3,000 dollar gap is mine, and the lender will see it. Rates and caps are commercial practice, not standards.
terms: Expected value — probability multiplied by impact, summed across outcomes; the long-run average cost of a risk.
Risk premium — the extra amount a party adds to its price for taking a risk, usually more than the risk's expected value.
Retained risk — a risk the owner keeps, which must be covered by contingency, equity or a guarantee.

hostile.q: You kept ground risk to save the premium. Show me the contingency that covers it, or I cut the loan.
hostile.a: It is in the budget as a separate ground allowance, not buried in general contingency. Our geotechnical engineer's expected cost is 350,000 dollars; we carry 600,000 dollars against it, and the severe case of 3,000,000 dollars is covered by committed equity above that, which I can evidence. If your monitor wants a different figure, I would like to see the reasoning, and I will adjust the allowance rather than argue about it.

title: How Courts Read the Clauses That Move Risk
summary: Risk clauses do not enforce themselves; courts read them, and they read them with suspicion. Exclusions need clear words, indemnities for your own negligence need explicit words, consequential loss has a narrower legal meaning than most people think, and liquidated damages fail if they are a penalty or if the owner caused the delay.
body:
A risk clause is only as strong as the way a court will read it. Courts read clauses that take away rights narrowly, so the words must be clear, and the party relying on them must not have caused the problem it is trying to avoid.

Recall

Q. What is expected value, as Roman used it?

A. Probability times impact, summed across outcomes: the long-run average cost of a risk, used to compare a risk premium with the cost of keeping the risk.

Q. In Week 77, what does a notice clause usually require?

A. Written notice, to a named person or address, in a stated form, within a stated time of the event or of when the party became aware of it. The detail matters, because a defective notice can be treated as no notice.

Q. In Week 70, what is an exemption from securities registration?

A. A route, set out in securities law, that allows securities to be sold without a full prospectus or registration, provided defined conditions about the investors, amounts or channels are met.

Why this matters

Mr Shabazz, the clause you negotiated is not the clause you will be held to. You will be held to the clause as a court, an arbitrator or a dispute board reads it, years later, with the loss already on the table. This lesson teaches how those readers think, so that you draft, and accept, clauses that survive the reading. These are general common-law concepts. The rules differ between jurisdictions, and some places have statutes that override the contract; verify that against the primary source before you rely on it.

Clear words, read against the drafter

In plain English: if a clause takes away a right, it had better say so plainly, and any doubt goes against the party who wrote it.

The professional framing has two parts. First, exclusion and limitation clauses are read strictly: they cover what they clearly cover and no more. Second, where a clause is genuinely ambiguous, many courts apply contra proferentem, reading it against the party that proposed it or relies on it. Commercial courts in several jurisdictions have narrowed this rule between sophisticated parties, but the direction of travel is the same: ambiguity is the drafter's problem.

Canada's Supreme Court set out a structured approach to exclusion clauses in Tercon Contractors v British Columbia in 2010: does the clause apply on its true reading; was it unconscionable when made; and is there an overriding public policy reason not to enforce it [unverified — confirm independently]. Other jurisdictions use different tests. The practical lesson is constant: write the clause so the first question has an obvious answer.

A worked example, hypothetical. A consultant's appointment says: liability shall not exceed the fee. The fee was 300,000 dollars, then grew to 450,000 dollars through additional services. Is the cap 300,000 or 450,000 dollars? Is it per claim or in total? Does it cover negligence? The clause does not say. A court may read the ambiguity against the consultant who relied on it. Better drafting removes the argument: total aggregate liability for all claims under or in connection with this appointment, including negligence, shall not exceed a stated fixed amount. The owner can still negotiate the number; at least both sides know what it is.

Indemnities and your own negligence

Owners like broad indemnities: the contractor shall indemnify the owner against all claims arising out of the works. Courts ask a sharp question of such words: do they cover losses caused by the owner's own negligence? The general common-law position is that an indemnity does not cover the indemnified party's own negligence unless the words say so clearly. Many American states go further, with statutes restricting or voiding construction indemnities for the indemnitee's sole negligence, and some for partial negligence [unverified — confirm independently]; verify that against the primary source before you rely on it.

So an owner who drafts a sweeping indemnity may find it unenforceable exactly where it was meant to bite. A clause that allocates loss in proportion to each party's fault, backed by insurance that names the owner, is often the stronger protection.

Say that out loud now.

A clause that takes away a right must say so plainly, or a court will read it away.

What consequential loss actually means

Most people think consequential loss means any loss that follows from a breach, such as lost rent. In the common law tradition the phrase has a narrower history. The English case of Hadley v Baxendale, in 1854, divided recoverable loss into two kinds: loss arising naturally, in the usual course of things, from the breach; and loss the parties could reasonably have contemplated as likely when they made the contract. Many courts have treated consequential loss as meaning only the second kind. On that reading, an exclusion of consequential loss may not exclude lost rent at all, if lost rent is the natural result of a late building.

That is why careful drafters do not rely on the phrase. They list what is excluded: loss of profit, loss of revenue, loss of rent, loss of use, financing costs. And they list what is not excluded, such as liquidated damages and amounts covered by insurance. A list removes the argument.

Liquidated damages: the penalty rule and the prevention principle

Liquidated damages are a sum fixed in advance for late completion. Two rules can defeat them.

The penalty rule. Courts will not enforce a sum that is a penalty rather than compensation. The traditional test asked whether the figure was a genuine pre-estimate of loss. The UK Supreme Court in Cavendish Square v Makdessi, in 2015, recast the test as whether the sum protects a legitimate interest and is not out of all proportion to it. Many American courts ask whether the sum was a reasonable forecast of harm that was hard to estimate. Other jurisdictions differ again; verify that against the primary source before you rely on it. The safe course in every system is the same: keep a dated calculation showing how you arrived at the daily rate.

The prevention principle. A party cannot hold the other to a completion date that it prevented the other from meeting. If the owner delays the contractor, by late drawings or late access, and the contract has no mechanism to extend time for owner-caused delay, the completion date can fall away, and with it the right to liquidated damages. Time may then be at large, meaning the contractor must finish within a reasonable time. The cure is a working extension-of-time clause that covers owner-caused delay, so the date moves and the liquidated damages survive.

A second worked example, hypothetical. Liquidated damages are 6,000 dollars a day. The contractor finishes 50 days late. The owner was 20 days late issuing structural drawings, and the contract has a proper extension-of-time clause. The completion date moves by 20 days, and the owner may claim 30 days, or 180,000 dollars. Without that clause, the owner might recover nothing in liquidated damages and be left proving general damages for whatever delay it can show was the contractor's.

Force majeure is a creature of contract

In common law systems there is no general doctrine of force majeure. Relief comes from the clause, and from it only. Read its list of events, whether the list is closed or open, what notice is required and what relief follows: time only, or time and money. Outside the clause sits frustration, which discharges a contract only when performance becomes impossible or radically different, and courts apply it rarely.

Professional sign-off required: lawyer, as construction counsel in the governing jurisdiction.

The biggest risk

The biggest risk is relying on a clause that a court will read narrowly or refuse to enforce: a vague cap, a sweeping indemnity, a bare consequential loss exclusion, a liquidated damages rate with no calculation behind it. The control is explicit drafting and a dated file showing how every number was set.

The beginner's mistake

The beginner assumes that a clause both parties signed will be enforced word for word. Signed is not the same as enforceable, and enforceable is not the same as clear.

Callback

In Week 20, I taught that contracts are formed by offer, acceptance and consideration, and that remedies follow breach. This lesson is the other end of that story: the remedy clauses, read under pressure. The parties who drafted for the reading, not only for the signing, are the ones whose remedies still work.

Recap

Exclusions and caps are read strictly and ambiguity goes against the drafter. Indemnities rarely cover your own negligence without clear words, and statutes may limit them. Consequential loss can mean less than you think, so list exclusions. Liquidated damages fail as penalties or through the prevention principle. Force majeure exists only as the clause gives it.

Next: Priya on The Numbers: reverse engineering a liquidated damages rate from the owner's true daily cost of delay.
checklist: Every cap I accept states a fixed amount, whether it is aggregate or per claim, and whether it covers negligence.
I do not rely on an indemnity to cover my own negligence unless counsel confirms the words and the local statute allow it.
Every consequential loss exclusion lists what it excludes and what it does not.
I keep a dated calculation behind every liquidated damages rate.
My contract extends time for owner-caused delay, so liquidated damages survive.
I have read the force majeure clause for its events, its notice and its relief.
Counsel in the governing jurisdiction has reviewed every risk clause.
head: Field checklist
speak: A risk clause is only as strong as the way a court will read it. Clauses that take away rights are read strictly, and ambiguity tends to go against the party that wrote them. So a cap must state a fixed amount, aggregate or per claim, and whether it covers negligence. An indemnity usually does not cover my own negligence without clear words, and some states limit construction indemnities by statute. Consequential loss can mean less than people think; since Hadley v Baxendale in 1854, many courts have read it narrowly, so I list what is excluded, like lost rent and financing costs. Liquidated damages fail if they are a penalty, so I keep a dated calculation of the rate, and they can fail through the prevention principle if I delayed the contractor and the contract cannot extend time. Force majeure exists only as the clause gives it. Every rule here differs by jurisdiction, so counsel checks it.
terms: Contra proferentem — the rule that a genuinely ambiguous clause is read against the party that proposed or relies on it.
Penalty rule — the principle that courts will not enforce a sum for breach that is out of proportion to the interest it protects.
Prevention principle — the rule that a party cannot enforce a deadline it prevented the other party from meeting.

hostile.q: Your liquidated damages are 10,000 dollars a day. Prove to me that is not a penalty.
hostile.a: Here is the dated calculation we made before tender: daily construction interest on the projected balance, extended lender and monitor fees, extended insurance, our own site and management costs, and lost net rent from the scheduled opening, each with its source. It totals more than 10,000 dollars a day, and we set the rate below it. If you think an input is wrong, show me which, and we can discuss it now rather than in a dispute.

title: Reverse Engineering a Liquidated Damages Rate
summary: Start from a liquidated damages rate already written into a contract and work backward to the daily cost of delay it implies. Then build the owner's true daily cost from interest, fees, insurance, management and lost rent, and see how much delay risk the owner has quietly kept.
body:
A liquidated damages rate is a statement about what one day of delay costs you. Work backward from the rate in a contract and you can see, in dollars, how much of your own delay risk you have kept without noticing.

Recall

Q. What two rules can defeat liquidated damages?

A. The penalty rule, if the sum is out of proportion to the interest it protects, and the prevention principle, if the owner caused delay and the contract has no way to extend time for it.

Q. In Week 76, the checkpoint for deals and people, what is a reservation price?

A. The worst terms you will accept before walking away, set in advance from your best alternative, and kept private.

Q. In Week 71, what is misrepresentation in an offering document?

A. A false or misleading statement of a material fact, or the omission of one needed to make the rest not misleading, which can give investors a right to damages or to unwind their investment.

Why this matters

Mr Shabazz, most owners pick a liquidated damages rate by copying the last project, or by asking what the contractor will accept. Both are guesses. The rate should come from your own numbers, because it is the only compensation you get for the contractor's delay, and because a court may ask how you arrived at it. Today we start from a finished outcome, a rate already in a signed contract, and work backward to what it really says. All figures are hypothetical round numbers. Rates, caps and percentages here are commercial practice, not standards.

Step 1: read what the signed rate implies

The finished outcome. A construction contract of 20,000,000 dollars, on a project costing 30,000,000 dollars in total. Liquidated damages are 5,000 dollars per calendar day of late completion, capped at 5 percent of the contract sum.

Work backward. The cap is 5 percent of 20,000,000 dollars, which is 1,000,000 dollars. Divide the cap by the rate: 1,000,000 divided by 5,000 is 200 days. So this contract says two things. One day of contractor delay costs the owner about 5,000 dollars. And after 200 days of delay, any further delay costs the contractor nothing more in liquidated damages. Write both down. They are the contract's claims about your business, and you need to test them.

Step 2: build the true daily cost of delay

Now build the owner's real cost of one day late, from the components a lender would recognise. Assume the building is nearly finished, so the construction loan is almost fully drawn.

ComponentWorkingPer day
Construction loan interest20,000,000 dollars at 7 percent a year, divided by 3653,836 dollars
Extended lender and monitor fees15,000 dollars a month, divided by 30500 dollars
Extended builder's risk insurance9,000 dollars a month, divided by 30300 dollars
Owner's own project management12,000 dollars a month, divided by 30400 dollars
Lost net rent in the first monthsstabilised net operating income of 2,190,000 dollars a year is 6,000 dollars a day; half the building would have been let early, so 50 percent3,000 dollars
Total8,036 dollars

Net operating income (NOI) is rent and other income less operating expenses, before debt service. Using it, rather than gross rent, avoids counting money you would have spent on operating the building anyway.

So the true cost of a day of delay is about 8,000 dollars, against a contract rate of 5,000 dollars. The contract leaves roughly 3,000 dollars a day with the owner from the first day.

Say that out loud now.

The rate is a claim about my business. I test it against my own daily cost.

Step 3: the delay the owner has silently kept

Run a delay of 120 days, all of it the contractor's fault.

  1. True cost: 120 days times 8,036 dollars is 964,320 dollars.
  2. Recovered: 120 days times 5,000 dollars is 600,000 dollars, inside the 1,000,000 dollar cap.
  3. Kept by the owner: 964,320 less 600,000, which is 364,320 dollars.

Now run 250 days.

  1. True cost: 250 times 8,036 is 2,009,000 dollars.
  2. Recovered: the rate would give 1,250,000 dollars, but the cap stops it at 1,000,000 dollars.
  3. Kept by the owner: 1,009,000 dollars.

Past day 200, every extra day costs the owner the full 8,036 dollars and the contractor nothing more. A contractor in trouble knows exactly where that line is. Once it is reached, the commercial pressure to finish disappears.

Step 4: what a defensible rate and cap would look like

Set the rate from the build-up. A rate close to 8,000 dollars a day is a genuine forecast of loss, which helps it survive a penalty challenge. A rate below it is lawful and simply leaves risk with you. A rate far above it invites the challenge.

Then test the cap against a plausible bad delay. Suppose your scheduler, looking at the critical path, judges that a severe but realistic contractor delay is 180 days. At 8,000 dollars a day that is 1,440,000 dollars. A cap of 7.5 percent of the contract, 1,500,000 dollars, covers it. Bidders will price a higher rate and cap, perhaps adding a few hundred thousand dollars to the bid. Compare that premium with the 364,320 dollars you keep on a 120-day delay at the old terms, and with the probability of a delay that long, before deciding. This is the expected-value comparison from Roman's lesson, applied to one clause.

Two practical notes. First, the daily cost changes over the job: early in construction the loan is lightly drawn and no rent was due, so delay is cheaper; at the end it is most expensive. Liquidated damages are measured against the completion date, so the end-of-job figure is the right one. Second, if the building opens in phases, consider separate rates and dates for each phase, so that a late final floor does not cost the same as a late whole building.

A third note, on what liquidated damages do not cover. They are usually the owner's exclusive remedy for delay, which means you cannot also claim your actual delay losses on top. If you want to keep a separate claim for some other loss, such as a tenant's claim against you for a late handover, the contract must say so. Read the exclusivity wording before you set the rate, because it decides whether the rate is a floor or the whole of your recovery.

Step 5: keep the working

File the table from Step 2, dated, with the source of each input: the loan term sheet for the rate, the lender's fee letter, the broker's quote for insurance extension, the pro forma for the NOI. If a contractor later argues that the rate is a penalty, this page is your evidence that it was a reasoned forecast made at the time.

Professional sign-off required: lawyer, on the enforceability of the rate and cap in the governing jurisdiction; scheduler, on the realistic range of delay.

The biggest risk

The biggest risk is a cap reached early: once delay passes the cap, the contractor has no further financial reason to hurry, and every day after it is yours. The control is a cap tested against a realistic severe delay from the schedule, not copied from the last project.

The beginner's mistake

The beginner counts gross rent as the cost of delay. Use net operating income, and only the share that would actually have been earned in the early months, or your rate overstates the loss and invites a penalty challenge.

Callback

In Week 40, the interest reserve was sized on the draw curve, with the loan close to fully drawn at the end of construction. The same fact drives this calculation: the last months of a project carry the highest daily interest, which is exactly when liquidated damages bite. One model should produce both numbers.

Recap

Divide the cap by the rate to find the day after which delay is free to the contractor. Build the true daily cost from interest, fees, insurance, management and net rent. The difference between that cost and the rate is the delay risk you kept. Set the rate from the build-up, test the cap against a realistic severe delay, and file the working.

Next: LEX in The Room: negotiating a limitation of liability with a design consultant.
checklist: I divide the cap by the rate to find the day delay becomes free to the contractor.
I build my true daily cost of delay from interest, fees, insurance, management and net rent.
I use net operating income, not gross rent, for lost income.
I use the end-of-construction loan balance for daily interest.
I test the cap against a realistic severe delay from the critical path.
I consider separate rates for separate phases.
I file the dated working with the source of every input.
head: Field checklist
speak: A liquidated damages rate is a claim about what one day of delay costs me, so I work backward from it. A 20,000,000 dollar contract with 5,000 dollars a day, capped at 5 percent, means 1,000,000 dollars of protection, which runs out after 200 days. Then I build my true daily cost: loan interest of about 3,836 dollars a day at the end of the job, 500 for lender fees, 300 for insurance, 400 for my own management, and 3,000 of lost net rent. That is about 8,000 dollars a day. So at 120 days late I lose about 964,000 and recover 600,000, keeping 364,000. Past day 200 every day costs me the full 8,000 and the contractor nothing. A defensible rate is set from that build-up, the cap is tested against a realistic severe delay, and the dated working goes on file in case anyone calls it a penalty. These rates are commercial practice, not standards.
terms: Daily cost of delay — the owner's actual cost of one extra day before completion, built from interest, fees, insurance, management and lost net income.
Liquidated damages cap — the maximum total liquidated damages payable, after which further delay carries no further liquidated damages.
Net operating income (NOI) — income from a property less its operating expenses, before debt service and income tax.

hostile.q: Your build-up says delay costs you 8,000 dollars a day. Why should I accept a rate that high?
hostile.a: Because it is what delay actually costs, and I can show you each input and its source. I am not asking you to carry more than that. If you think an input is wrong, tell me which. If the issue is your exposure rather than the rate, I would rather discuss the cap, or an early completion incentive, than set a rate that leaves me carrying your delay.

title: Negotiating the Cap With Your Architect
summary: A scene: the design consultant's appointment caps liability at the fee and excludes consequential loss, and the principal wants to sign today. You need a cap that matches real exposure without breaking the relationship. The lines to say, the lines never to say, and the question behind the question.
body:
When a consultant asks for a low liability cap, the real issue is usually not the cap. It is the consultant's insurance. Negotiate the cap against the insurance, and the conversation becomes practical instead of personal.

Recall

Q. In Priya's reverse engineering, what does the liquidated damages cap divided by the daily rate tell you?

A. The number of days of delay after which further delay costs the contractor nothing more, so every day past it falls entirely on the owner.

Q. In Week 76, what does acknowledge, bridge, answer mean for a hostile question?

A. Acknowledge the concern behind the question, bridge to the facts that matter, then answer directly, without defensiveness and without evasion.

Q. In Week 71, what is a fiduciary duty?

A. A duty to act in another person's interest, with loyalty and care, which forbids putting your own interest first where the relationship carries that duty, as many sponsor and investor relationships can.

Why this matters

Mr Shabazz, a design consultant's error is one of the largest uninsured risks an owner carries, because the consultant's appointment usually limits what you can recover, and most owners sign that appointment early, in a hurry, before any design exists. Today's scene is that signing meeting. The numbers are hypothetical.

The scene

A project of 25,000,000 dollars. You are appointing the architect, who will lead the design team. The draft appointment, on the architect's own form, caps total liability at the fee, 900,000 dollars, and excludes consequential loss without a list. The principal, whom you respect and want to work with, says: this is our standard; every client signs it; our insurers require it. Your project manager wants the appointment signed today so design can start.

The question behind the question

The principal is not trying to escape responsibility for bad work. A design practice's real protection is its professional indemnity insurance: a policy that pays for claims of negligent professional advice or design. A cap at the fee keeps the practice's exposure inside what that policy will pay. If you demand unlimited liability, the practice faces a risk its insurance will not cover, and its own survival is at stake. So the question behind the question is: will you protect our insurance? Answer that question and the cap stops being a fight.

Your own question behind the question is different. You need to know what a serious design error would cost you, and how much of that you could actually collect.

The lines to say

Open with the shared interest. "I want this appointment to work for both of us, and I understand your cap protects your insurance. Can we build it around the insurance itself?"

Ask for the facts. "What is your professional indemnity limit, is it per claim or aggregate, and how much of the aggregate has already been used this year?" A policy with an aggregate limit can be eroded by other clients' claims, which matters to you.

Propose the structure. "Let's set the cap at a fixed figure equal to your per-claim limit, say 5,000,000 dollars, rather than the fee. You keep the policy in force at that level through completion and for a stated number of years after, and you give us a certificate each year."

On consequential loss. "I can accept an exclusion of lost profit and lost rent if it is listed. I cannot accept the cost of correcting your own design, or the cost of other consultants redesigning around an error, being treated as consequential."

A worked example the principal will follow. A coordination error between structure and services forces rework costing 1,800,000 dollars. Under the draft, recovery stops at 900,000 dollars. Under the proposal, rework is a direct loss within a 5,000,000 dollar cap, covered by the policy. Nothing in the proposal costs the practice more than its insurance pays.

Say that out loud now.

I am not asking you to go beyond your insurance. I am asking you to stop at it, not at your fee.

The lines never to say

Never say: "If you are confident in your work, you will not need a cap." It is an insult dressed as logic, and every professional hears it that way. Competent people make errors; that is why the insurance exists.

Never say: "Fine, we'll sign today and sort it out later." There is no later. Once design starts, your leverage falls every week.

Never say: "Our lawyer insists." Own the position. Hiding behind counsel makes you look as if you do not understand your own deal, and invites the principal to go around you.

When to stay silent

After you have proposed the 5,000,000 dollar structure, stop talking. The principal will need to think about the insurance. Silence lets that thinking happen. If you fill the pause, you will usually fill it with a concession.

Stay silent, too, if the principal says the insurers would need to confirm. That is not a refusal. It is the beginning of the right conversation. Agree a date for the answer and write it down.

Holding your state

You will feel pressure to sign because design has a schedule and the team is waiting. Name it to yourself: this is the planning fallacy from Week 3, the belief that a delay of a week will cost more than it does. One week of negotiation against a project of years is cheap. Keep your voice low and slow. Treat the principal as a partner in the problem, because they are.

A second worked example, on the timing trade. A week's delay to the design start costs, in your model, perhaps 20,000 dollars in carrying cost on the land. The difference between a 900,000 dollar cap and a 5,000,000 dollar cap is 4,100,000 dollars of protection on a risk that is real. That trade is not close.

Working with advisers

This week's monthly thread is how you use your advisers. Your lawyer will mark up the appointment; your broker should tell you what professional indemnity limits are realistic for a practice of this size. Brief both before the meeting, with the same one-page allocation matrix, so they are solving the same problem rather than each defending their own corner.

Then make the decision yourself. Advisers tell you what a clause means and what the market accepts. Only you decide how much risk your project should carry. If you find yourself signing because an adviser said it was fine, without being able to say why it is fine, stop and ask the question again.

Professional sign-off required: lawyer, on the appointment; insurance broker, on professional indemnity limits and terms.

The biggest risk

The biggest risk is signing the consultant's standard appointment early, under schedule pressure, with a cap at the fee and an undefined consequential loss exclusion. The control is to negotiate the cap against the consultant's insurance before design starts, and to list exactly what is excluded.

The beginner's mistake

The beginner fights for unlimited liability. That fight is usually lost, and even when won it is worth little, because a practice's real capacity to pay is its insurance. Fight for a fixed cap that matches the insurance, and for the insurance to stay in force.

Callback

In Week 66, Kema and JAX taught interests versus positions. The fee cap is a position. The interest behind it is protecting the practice's insurance. Your position is unlimited liability; your interest is being able to recover a real loss. The 5,000,000 dollar structure serves both interests, which is why it can be agreed.

Recap

The consultant's cap protects its insurance. Ask for the policy limits and terms, set the cap as a fixed figure matched to the per-claim limit, keep the policy in force after completion, and list the consequential loss exclusions. Say the shared interest, avoid the insult, stay silent after the proposal, and do not let schedule pressure set your price.

Next: Kema on the Week 78 review: six questions, a Red Pen drill on a risk clause and the boardroom drill.
checklist: I read the consultant's appointment before design starts, not after.
I ask for the professional indemnity limit, per claim and aggregate, and how much is used.
I propose a fixed cap matched to the per-claim insurance limit, not the fee.
I require the policy to stay in force after completion for a stated period.
I accept a consequential loss exclusion only as a list.
I keep the cost of correcting the consultant's own design as a direct loss.
I brief my lawyer and broker with the same allocation matrix before the meeting.
I stay silent after making my proposal.
head: Field checklist
speak: When a design consultant asks for a liability cap at its fee, the real issue is its insurance. A practice's protection is its professional indemnity policy, and a cap at the fee keeps its exposure inside what that policy pays. So I do not fight for unlimited liability. I ask for the policy limits, per claim and aggregate, and how much has been used. Then I propose a fixed cap equal to the per-claim limit, say 5,000,000 dollars on a 25,000,000 dollar project, with the policy kept in force after completion. I accept a consequential loss exclusion only as a list, and I keep the cost of correcting the consultant's own design as a direct loss. I never say that a confident firm would not need a cap. I stay silent after my proposal. And I remember that a week of negotiation is cheap against a 4,000,000 dollar difference in protection.
terms: Professional indemnity insurance — insurance that pays claims against a professional for negligent advice or design.
Aggregate limit — the most an insurance policy will pay for all claims in a policy period, which other claims can erode.
Run-off cover — insurance kept in force after the work ends, so claims made later are still covered.

hostile.q: Every client signs our standard cap at the fee. Why should you be different?
hostile.a: Because the fee is the wrong measure. A coordination error on a building this size could cost more than twice your fee to fix, and I could only recover half of it. I am not asking you to go beyond your insurance. I am asking you to set the cap at your per-claim limit and keep the policy in force after completion. That costs you nothing your insurer has not already priced, and it means a real error does not end up as a dispute between us.

role: Chief of staff and learning coach
title: Week 78 Review: Who Pays When It Goes Wrong
summary: Six questions test the week: the allocation test, expected cost against a risk premium, how courts read caps and indemnities, consequential loss, liquidated damages and the consultant's cap. A Red Pen drill on a hypothetical risk clause, then a two-minute boardroom drill.
body:
This week came down to one sentence: every risk has an owner, the contract names it, and the right owner is the party that can control it, price it and carry it.

Recall

Q. What is the question behind a consultant's request for a cap at its fee?

A. Will you protect our insurance? The answer is a fixed cap matched to the per-claim professional indemnity limit, with the policy kept in force.

Q. In Week 77, what are ConsensusDocs?

A. A family of American standard construction contract forms, produced by a coalition of industry organisations as an alternative to the AIA documents, often described as aiming for a more balanced allocation of risk.

Q. In Week 71, what should investor reporting always include?

A. Honest, regular, consistent information on performance against plan, cash, risks and material changes, delivered on the schedule promised, including bad news as early as good news.

Why this matters

Mr Shabazz, if you can answer these six questions aloud without notes, you can read any risk clause in a construction contract and know what it is doing to your money. Answer each before reading the answer.

The six questions

Question 1. State the allocation test.

Answer: Give each risk to the party that can best control it, price it and carry it. Where nobody passes all three, share it or insure it. Pay openly for every risk you move.

Question 2. Bidders want 750,000 dollars to take a ground risk with an expected cost of 350,000 dollars. Do you transfer it?

Answer: Usually not, because the premium is more than twice the expected cost. The exception is when the worst case would break the project; then you pay to move it, to a party that can actually carry it.

Question 3. Why might a broad indemnity fail to protect the owner?

Answer: Because courts usually read an indemnity as not covering the indemnified party's own negligence unless the words say so clearly, some statutes limit construction indemnities, and an indemnity is worth only what the other party can pay.

Question 4. Why do careful drafters list what a consequential loss exclusion covers?

Answer: Because in the common law tradition, since Hadley v Baxendale in 1854, consequential loss has often been read narrowly, so a bare exclusion may not exclude lost rent or profit. A list removes the argument.

Question 5. A contract has liquidated damages of 5,000 dollars a day capped at 1,000,000 dollars, and your true daily cost of delay is 8,000 dollars. What does it tell you?

Answer: You keep about 3,000 dollars a day from the first day, and after 200 days delay costs the contractor nothing more, so every further day costs you the full 8,000 dollars.

Question 6. What is the prevention principle?

Answer: A party cannot enforce a completion date it prevented the other from meeting. If the owner delays the contractor and the contract cannot extend time for it, the date and the liquidated damages can fall away.

Say that out loud now.

Recap of the week

LEX set out the allocation test and the six tools. Ford and Cole took a composite case of a ground clause that transferred everything, and gave Rule 78. Roman priced risk transfer against expected cost and the receiving party's capacity. LEX showed how courts read the clauses. Priya reverse engineered a liquidated damages rate. LEX negotiated a consultant's cap against its insurance.

The Red Pen

Read this hypothetical clause from an owner's draft construction contract and find the defects before reading on.

Clause 14. The Contractor shall indemnify the Owner against all claims whatsoever arising from the Works. The Contractor's liability is limited to the Contract Sum. Neither party is liable for consequential loss. The Contractor accepts all risk of ground conditions, whether or not shown in the Owner's reports, which are provided for information only and on which the Contractor may not rely. Liquidated damages for delay are 15,000 dollars per day. Force majeure means any event beyond the Contractor's control.

The defects. First, the indemnity covers all claims whatsoever, which on most readings will not cover the owner's own negligence without explicit words, and may be limited by statute where the project sits; it promises more than it delivers. Second, the cap is the contract sum, but it does not say whether it is aggregate or per claim, whether it covers negligence, or whether liquidated damages and the indemnity sit inside it. Third, the consequential loss exclusion has no list, so nobody knows whether lost rent is excluded, and it is mutual, which may strip the owner of its own delay losses. Fourth, the ground clause moves all ground risk to the contractor and also tells it not to rely on the owner's reports, which invites high bids, invites a challenge if the reports were inaccurate, and fails Rule 78. Fifth, the liquidated damages rate has no cap and no stated basis, which makes it look like a penalty unless the owner can show a calculation, and there is no extension-of-time mechanism, so the prevention principle could defeat it. Sixth, force majeure is defined only as events beyond the contractor's control, with no list, no notice requirement and no statement of relief, so it could cover almost anything, including the contractor's own subcontractor failing.

Then ask what each fix costs. Narrowing the indemnity and listing the exclusions costs nothing. Taking ground risk back lowers bids but needs a ground allowance in your budget. Setting a reasoned liquidated damages rate with a cap may raise the bid a little. Write each change against its price.

The boardroom drill

Stand up and explain this week to an investment committee in two minutes. Start a timer.

Model answer: "Every construction contract is a decision about who pays when something goes wrong. We give each risk to the party that can control it, price it and carry it. The contractor carries workmanship, sequence and safety. We keep ground risk, because we commissioned the investigation and know more about the site than a bidder can in a tender period; we have a separate ground allowance against it, sized on our engineer's expected cost with equity behind the severe case. Our consultants' liability is capped at their professional indemnity limits, not their fees, with the policies kept in force after completion. Liquidated damages are set from our own daily cost of delay, about 8,000 dollars a day at the end of the job, with a cap tested against a realistic severe delay. Every exclusion is a list, and every risk clause has been reviewed by construction counsel. The result is lower bids, fewer disputes, and a contingency the lender can see is sized to the risks we actually kept."

Score your answer. Did you lead with the allocation principle? Did you name at least one risk you kept, and how it is covered? Did you put a number on delay? Did you finish inside two minutes? If not, record it again tomorrow.

The biggest risk

The biggest risk this week is believing that signing a clause moves a risk. A risk moves only to a party that can carry it, under words a court will enforce. The control is the allocation test, explicit drafting and a credit check on every party you transfer risk to.

The beginner's mistake

Memorising the six tools without asking of each one: what does it cover, and how much? Every risk clause has two axes, and the second one decides your money.

Callback

In Week 2, Ford and I taught the pre-mortem: imagine the project has failed, then explain why. Run one on your contract. Imagine the dispute is already under way, and ask which clause the other side is reading. That clause is the one to fix before you sign.

Recap

Allocate each risk to the party that can control, price and carry it. Compare the premium with the expected cost, and ask whether you can survive the bad case. Draft caps, indemnities and exclusions so a court can read them plainly. Set liquidated damages from your own numbers. Negotiate consultants' caps against their insurance. Rule 78 keeps risk with the party that can manage it.

head: The six questions
speak: Every construction contract decides who pays when something goes wrong. The right owner of a risk can control it, price it and carry it. A risk pushed onto someone who cannot carry it comes back as a premium in the bid and then as a claim or an insolvency. So I compare the premium with the expected cost of keeping the risk, and separately ask whether I can survive the worst case. Courts read risk clauses strictly: caps must say how much and for what, indemnities rarely cover my own negligence without clear words, and consequential loss exclusions should be lists. Liquidated damages are set from my own daily cost of delay, with a cap tested against a realistic delay and a way to extend time for my own delays, or the prevention principle can defeat them. Consultants' caps are matched to their insurance, not their fee. Rule 78: never transfer a risk to a party that cannot control, price or carry it.
terms: Allocation matrix — a table listing each significant risk against each party, with who controls, prices and carries it.
Extension-of-time clause — a clause that moves the completion date for defined causes of delay, including the owner's own.
Mutual exclusion — an exclusion that applies to both parties, which can remove the owner's own recovery as well as the contractor's.

hostile.q: Your clause 14 indemnifies you against all claims whatsoever. Isn't that the strongest protection you could have?
hostile.a: It reads as the strongest and may enforce as the weakest. A court is unlikely to read it as covering our own negligence, a statute may limit it, and it is worth only what the contractor can pay. We have replaced it with a fault-based indemnity, backed by insurance that names us, with limits matched to the exposure. It is narrower on paper and stronger in practice.
